 HOUSTON COUNTY, Ga. (WGXA) — State health officials believe a person diagnosed with measles in Macon County may have exposed others to the disease at a restaurant in Perry, Ga.
 The Georgia Department of Public Health (DPH) announced on Monday that it determined that the Macon County patient diagnosed with measles visited the Longhorn Steakhouse at 100 Hampton Court in Perry, and said patrons who were there on Oct. 7 from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m. could be infected.
 Visitors to the Longhorn Steakhouse along Hampton Court during the exposure window are urged to check their vaccination status and watch out for measles symptoms.
 DPH said the symptoms usually appear within one to two weeks after exposure but could take up to 21 days, and include high fever, cough, runny nose and watery eyes that are followed by a red rash that begins on the head and spreads to the rest of the body.
 Officials said the disease is "highly contagious," spreading through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and it can remain airborne for up to two hours after the infected person leaves.
 READ MORE | President Trump to rally in Macon just over a week out from midterm elections 
 Anyone with measles symptoms is advised to contact their healthcare provider immediately. DPH emphasized the importance of not going to a doctor's office, hospital, or public health clinic without calling ahead to report the symptoms.
 DPH said the MMR vaccine is the "best protection against measles."
